Bay of Algieri July 4th, 1815. þÿSir We have the honor to refer you to the official reports of Commodore Decatur to the navy department for ail account of the operations of this squadron previous to our arrival off Algiers, on the þÿ28" ult. Having received information that the Algerine squadron had been at sea for a considerable time longer than that to which their cruisers usually extend, and that a dispatch boat had been sent from Gibraltar to Algiers, to inform them of our arrival in the Mediterranean, we thought that they might have made a harbour, where they would be in safety. We, therefore, whilst they were in this state of uncertainty, believed it a proper moment to deliver the þÿPresident letter, s agreeably to our instructions. Accordingly on the 29th ult. a flag of truce was hoisted on board the Guerriere, with the Swedish flag at tin main. A boat came off about noon, with Mr. þÿN oderling, consul of Sweden, and the captain of the port, who confirmed the intelligence we had before received, and to whom we communicated information of the capture of their frigate and brig The impression made by these events was visible and deep. We were requested by the eapt. of the port, Mr. Norderiing, declaring he was not authorized to act, to state the conditions on which we would makepeace, to which we replied, by giving the letter of

the President to the Dey, and by a note from us to him, a copy of which (No. 1) we have the honor to transmit herewith. The Captain of tlio port then requested that hostilities should cease, pending the negoeiation, and that persons authorised to treat should go on shore, he and Air. Norderiing both affirming that the minister of marine had pledged himself for our security and return to our ships when we pleased. Doth Those propositions were rejected, and they were explicitly itiformet that the negoeiation must be carried on on board the fleet, and that hostilities, as tar as they respected vessels, could not þÿcease. They returned on shore. On the following day the same persons returned and informed us that they were commissioned by the Dey to treat with us on the proposed basis, and their anxiety appeared extreme to conclude the peace immediately. We then brought forward the model of a treaty, which we declared would not be departed from in substance, at the same time declaring that although the United 'dal.s would never stipulate for paying tribute under any form whatever, yet that they were a magnanimous stud generous nation, who would, upon the presentation of consuls, do what was customary with other great nations, m

ttieir friendly intercourse with Alg:e>s.« The treaty was then examinoti, nnd they were of opinion, that it would not be agreed to in its present form, and particularly requested that the article requiring the restitution of the property they had captured, and which had been distributed, might he expunged, alleging that such a demand had never before been made upou Algiers, To this it was answered that the claim was just and would he adhered to. They then asked, wlir. thee, it the treaty should be signed by the Dey, we would engage to restore the captured vessels; which we refused. They then represented that it was not the present Dey who had declared the war, which they acknowledged to be unjust, conced. iug that they were wholly in the wrong, and had no excuse, and requested that we woidd take the ease of the Dey into consideration, and upon his agreeing to terms with us more favorable than had ever been made with any other nation, to restore the ships, which they stated would he of little or no value to us, but would be of great importance to him, as they would satisfy the people with the conditions of the peace we were going to conclude with him. M e consulted upon this question, and determined that, considering the stateoi those vessels, the sains that would be required to fit them for a passage to the United States, and the little probability of selling them in this part of the world, we would make a compliment of them to his highness i" <he state they then were, the commodore

engaging to furnish them with an escort to this port. This, however, would depend upon their signing the treaty as presented j to them, and could not appear as an arti- J cle of it, but must be considered ns a favor conferred on the Dey by die United States. They then requested a truce, to deliberate upon the terms o( the proposed treaty which was refused ; they even pleaded for three hours. The reply wa þÿ not a minute; if your squadron appears in sight before the treaty is actually signed Ivy the Dey, and die prisoners sent off, ours would capture þÿthem. It was finally agreed that hostilities should cease when we perceived their boat coming off with a white flag hoisted, the Swedish consul pledging his word of honour not to hoist it unless the treaty was signed, and the prisoners in the boat. They returned on shore, and þÿaltho the distance was full five miles, they came back within three hours, with the treaty signed, as we had concluded it, and the prisoners. During the interval of their absence a corvette appeared in sight, which would have been captured if they had been detained one liour longer. The treaty has since been drawn out anew, translated by them, and duly executed by the Dey, which we have the honor to transmit herewith. Mr. Shaler has since been on shore, and th« cotton and money mentioned in the 4th article, have been given up to him. þÿI>< now / show every disposition to w;ua-
I doubtless, owing to the tain & sincere pence with us, which a dread of our arms ;

in our opinion, the only secure guarantee we can have for the maintenance of the peace just concluded with these people, is the presence, in the Meditteranean, of a respectable naval force. As this treaty appears to us to secure every interest within the contemplation of the government, and as it really places the U. States on higher ground than any other nation, we have no hesitation, on our part, in fulfilling such of its provisions as are within our power, in the firm belief that it will receive the ratification of the President and Senate. We have the honor to he, with respect, Sir, your obedient servants, SHIPMENT DECATUR. WILLIAM SHALER.

The undersigned have the honor to inform his highness the Dey of Algiers, that they have be. u appointed by the President of the United Slates of America, Commissioners Plenipotentiary to treat of Peace with his Highness, and that pursuant to their instructions, they are ready to open a negoeiation for the restoration of peace and harmony between the two countries on terms just and honorable to both parties ; and they feel it incumbent on them to state explicitly to his highness, that they are instructed to treat upon no other priuciple, than that of perfect equality, and on the terms of the most favored nations; no stipulation for paying any tribute to Algiers, under any form whatever, will be ftgreed to. The undersigned have the honour to transmit herewith, a letter from the President of lie United States, and they avail themselves of this occasion to assure his highness, of the highest consideration and profound respect.

At the moment he was driving off, another farmer stepped up and told them that lie would give each reaper (id. a day more than the pei-son they had engaged with, if they would quit their pteseui master and enter his service. Allured by /his offer, jliey all engaged with the best bidder, except one woman, who went home with her master, and at night received a guinea for her day's wages, tins circumstance she did not fail to communicate to those who had gone to work for the other farmer, under the promise ot an additional six-pence a day; they all of course, insisted upon a fulfilment of the agreement ; and the farmer, after having been summoned before a magistrate, was obliged to pay each of his laborers 2D, tik. pegday.

One of the most important public record of many years, ami which cannot be too well known, is now in circulation amongst the Members of Parliament in confidence of Govermnf nt ; and we must express our regret, that it has been hitherto confined to tins partial publicity. Upon the fit at appearance of the present device of public distress, the Government, with a laudable anxiety of procuring authentic reports from the different counties of the kingdom, applied to the Hoard 0t Agriculture, requesting the Members of that Boaid to employ their means of information and correspondence m procuring these accounts. As the best method f effecting this purpose, the Board composed a long" string of questions, and transmitting them to their usual correspondents, and in some instances to the clergy and magistrates of counties, requested answers to them in detail and particulars. These answers were accordingly sent, and having been all collected in the month of April last, were sent to press, and printed in a large octavo vo_ fume. The first intention was to circulate this book in the same manner as the Parliamentary Reports, but this purpose was immediately abandoned, and a very private circulation, confined merely to the Ministers and the þÿMinisters friends, substituted in its stead. Upon seeing the nature ol this work, we must commend the prudence of the Ministers in tin immediate suppression, as far as respected general circulation. þÿ Many of the Reports are, indeed, of a ve-

ry intelligent and valuable nature, and by themselves could not bo too generally circulated. Others are fritolous, ignorant, and factious; many of them highly malicious, and the writers of still more of them seem eagerly to have availed themselves of an opportunity assailing every of Hvtnblishment in the State, þÿ in a word, employing their Reports as means of lihellling the Church and State, and conveying their private malice under the cover of a Memoir for the Public good. Hut tliis mixture does not destroy the value of the better articles, and we must Repeat, our regret, that instead of publishing, without separation or discrimination, the. whole of what they have collected, the Board <»f Agriculture did not make a due selection oi 0 þÿ die! not elect those Reports of the Clergy, Magistrates, and Gentlemen of property, who, writing under Pie habitual impression of their own diameter and respectability, were careful to confine themselves to the points ami object of the Government, and to observe the, restraints of decorum, and private lights. As wr; hope to sec this suggestion followed up, we shall contiue outsdres, for

the present, with the mere enumeration of the hearts under which these Reports distribute the causes of our present National Distress. Our readers rr ill see that they add little, perhaps nothing, to wlmt we have ourselves repeatedly said; but as they speak from practical knowledge they may serve to couth m it. 1. The first cause of our present distress must he sought in that unexampled pros- i peril y, that forced elevation, to which we were raised by the events of the wars of the French Revolution in its commence- j inent. The destruction of the þÿenemy co- s j lollies and commerce threw all the colon- j ial commerce, aud nearly all the rontineu- ! tal commerce ot t lie world in our hands. Hence at this period (1793 4, and the sue. ceeding years) the unexampled growth of commerce, our manufactures, and, through them, of our agriculture. 2. The scarcity of 1700' and ol I800still further augmented our Agricultuie, by causing such prices as brought all the pooiesl land of the kingdom into cultivation. the annual agricultural product of the kingdom has thus been augmented by nearly one third, and if we add to this cause, the increased productiveness ol the land, by mors expensive cultivation, and by general inclosures, the increase ot annual agricultural produce, may be rated nearly at one halt. 3 T lie immence expenditure of Government (so many millions being raised by tnxeg, and distributed amongst tiie markets) concurred to the same nd5 tbeir great purchases raised the price of

corn and encouraged cultivation; and the vast sum of money, no mailer whether of paper or coin, thus thrown juo the mar- i ket, created a real encouragement to colli- i merce and agriculture, and a seeming ; plenty and afiiuence throughout the kingdom. 4. The suspension ef cash payments by the Hank, added to these effects. Paper Credit, Discount, and Accommodation, was extenileded throughout the kingdom; the national capital was doubled, and Agriculture and Commerce assisted in the same proportion. 5. Tile acquisition of all the þÿenemy Co- s lonies, and the effect of the Berlin and Milan Decrees, completed thischain of causes, the one giving us all the Colonial Trade, and the other establishing our commercial monopoly. All the commerce of the wot Id was then truly in our hands þÿ our agriculture rose in proportion þÿ our population j followed in the same degree. 6. To these general causes of our unexampled prosperity, are to be added what certainly resulted from them, hut what is of itself of sufficient importance to he en- i tilled a cause in itself, þÿ namely, the vast j increase and improvement ot our machinery. 7. As such were the causes of our unexampled prosperity, so the causes of our present decline are, first, (in some degree) the operation of these causes; and secondly, and most materially, the absence aud forcible leinovfcl of them.

8 The effects of the extraordinary encouragement of our Agriculture were no sooner þÿfelt,- our produce was no sooner augmented, by bringing all our foimer barrens into fertility, than the country was bli sed by a succession of ihe best harvests ever known, llonce an abundance þÿ .finitelybeyond the w ish of the farmer, and beyond the demand of the þÿcountry, -. Hence a glut of thr market, and an immediate forcible deprea ion of prices. Such Was the instanl effect ol the plenty oftho yeais 1812 and IHI3 9. I be fall of the Emperor Napoleon, arid the certainty of Peace, added to this elb'Cf ; Government þÿiniui.xlint |y itlmiu. islied their expenditure, that is, their purchases in tiie corn, cattle, and other markets, by at least, forty millions in the year, and the consumption, and consequent demand of the Country, instantly fell from the Vt iij- standard to the low Peace average. 10.
